title: ABM Pilot (Regulated Workloads) — Persona Objections & Answers (Draft Q&A Matrix)
content:
Last updated: 2026-02-11 (owner: Soojin)

Purpose
- Fast, consistent answers for the ABM regulated pilot (FinServ + Healthcare) across CISO/GRC/Platform/ML personas.
- Keep language aligned to approved Security/GRC positioning. If a prospect asks for something outside what’s listed as “Supported today,” route to Security/GRC for a precise response.

How to use this doc
- Each section is written as “Objection / Question → Crisp answer (what to say) → Follow-ups / evidence to offer → Guardrails (what NOT to say) → Who to pull in.”
- Default CTA in regulated conversations: “Happy to schedule a 30-min security + architecture review; we’ll bring Security and SE and share our questionnaire-ready responses.”

Global guardrails (read first)
- Don’t over-promise roadmap (especially around on-prem packaging maturity, retention controls beyond current capabilities, or any certs not explicitly confirmed by GRC).
- Don’t imply “we never store anything” unless scoped precisely to a deployment mode and a specific log configuration. Use the approved residency/retention language.
- If asked “Are you HIPAA compliant?” / “Will you sign a BAA?” / “Are you PCI compliant?”: acknowledge the requirement, state what we support operationally (controls, auditability, deployment isolation), and move to the formal process (Legal + Security) without making blanket compliance claims.

Approved references (use these links when sharing collateral)
- Core messaging framework (approved phrases + risky claims): confluence:sales-enablement/positioning-and-messaging/vertical-abm-regulated-workloads-core-messaging
- FinServ Security FAQ addendum (questionnaire-ready language): confluence:sales-enablement/security-faq/abm-finserv-security-faq-addendum
- Healthcare Security FAQ addendum (PHI-specific assumptions + language): confluence:sales-enablement/security-faq/abm-healthcare-security-faq-addendum
- Retention + residency positioning (what’s supported today + safe phrasing): confluence:security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/abm-pilot-retention-and-residency-positioning
- Private/VPC reference architecture (network boundaries + responsibilities): confluence:eng-private-deployments/reference-architectures/private-vpc-reference-architecture-regulated-workloads
- Competitive battlecard (landmines + when to walk away): confluence:sales-enablement/competitive/regulated-inference-competitive-battlecard

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PERSONA: CISO / Head of Security

1) “We can’t send sensitive data (PHI/PII/financial) to a shared hosted LLM endpoint.”
What to say
- Redwood supports multiple deployment modes so regulated teams can match data sensitivity and risk posture: Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private (VPC / on-prem options).
- For highly sensitive workloads, we generally recommend Redwood Private in your VPC (or dedicated isolated environment) so you control network boundaries and can align with internal policies.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Offer the Private/VPC reference architecture and a security + architecture review.
- Share the relevant Security FAQ addendum (FinServ or Healthcare).
Guardrails
- Don’t imply that Hosted is “non-compliant.” Frame it as “deployment choice based on data classification + controls required.”
- Don’t promise on-prem for every timeline; validate requirements and loop in Private product owner.
Pull in
- Dr. Aisha Rahman (CISO), Kevin Osei (FAQs), Simran Kaur / Colin O’Donnell (Private discovery)

2) “Do you store our prompts/outputs? What’s your retention policy?”
What to say
- We can walk through our data handling by deployment mode and the specific logging configuration. We’ll be explicit about what is processed transiently for serving, what is logged for operations, and what can be configured/limited.
- For regulated customers, we align retention with operational needs and provide options for exporting audit logs to customer-controlled systems.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Use the approved internal guidance as the source of truth during Q&A: confluence:security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/abm-pilot-retention-and-residency-positioning
- Offer to provide questionnaire-ready responses under NDA if needed.
Guardrails
- Don’t say “we don’t store anything” or “zero retention” unless Security confirms exact configuration + product behavior for the prospect’s deployment mode.
Pull in
- Olga Petrov (GRC), Marcus Lin (Security Eng), Kevin Osei

3) “We need audit logs we can export to our SIEM (Splunk/Sentinel) with retention controls.”
What to say
- Redwood supports audit logging and provides export/integration patterns so customers can centralize events in their SIEM.
- In Private/VPC deployments, audit and operational logs can be routed into customer-controlled logging pipelines based on the reference architecture.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Share Security FAQ addendum; point to the logging/audit pipeline section in the Private reference architecture.
- Ask which SIEM and preferred formats (JSON, syslog, webhook) and whether they require immutable storage / WORM.
Guardrails
- Don’t claim “native Splunk app” or specific turnkey connectors unless confirmed. Use “export patterns / integration options.”
Pull in
- Markus Klein / Fatima Noor (SE), Marcus Lin

4) “How do you handle encryption and key management? We require customer-managed keys (CMK) and possibly HSM.”
What to say
- Redwood supports encryption in transit and at rest and can integrate with customer key management requirements in Private/VPC contexts. We can align to your KMS/HSM policies based on deployment model.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Offer a dedicated session to map KMS/HSM requirements to the architecture (KMS type, rotation requirements, separation of duties).
- Point to Security FAQ addendum for approved wording.
Guardrails
- Don’t promise “HSM required/available everywhere” or name specific integrations as GA unless confirmed. Use “integration options based on environment.”
Pull in
- Marcus Lin, Simran Kaur, Colin O’Donnell

5) “Where is data processed? We have residency requirements (US-only / EU-only).”
What to say
- Redwood can support region-based deployments depending on the chosen mode. For strict residency, we typically recommend Private/VPC or dedicated region selection to meet policy requirements.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Use the approved residency language: confluence:security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/abm-pilot-retention-and-residency-positioning
Guardrails
- Don’t say “we support any region” or “country-level residency” unless confirmed for the specific request.
Pull in
- Olga Petrov, Markus Klein

6) “Do you have SOC 2? Can you share the report?”
What to say
- We can share our current compliance posture and the process for providing reports under NDA, as applicable.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Direct them to Security for sharing policy; offer a security review call where we can walk through controls.
Guardrails
- Don’t claim a specific certification level, scope, or report type in writing unless it’s in the approved FAQ.
Pull in
- Dr. Aisha Rahman, Olga Petrov

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PERSONA: GRC / Compliance / Risk

1) “We need clear responsibility boundaries (who operates what) for Private/VPC.”
What to say
- Redwood Private is designed with explicit shared responsibility. We’ll document what Redwood operates (runtime/software, updates per agreement) vs what you operate (networking, IAM policies, SIEM storage, etc.) depending on the deployment.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Share Private/VPC reference architecture and highlight the responsibilities section.
Guardrails
- Don’t imply “Redwood manages everything” in a customer VPC; keep it precise.
Pull in
- Simran Kaur, Colin O’Donnell, Olga Petrov

2) “We need to complete a security questionnaire quickly—do you have standard answers?”
What to say
- Yes—Redwood has questionnaire-ready language for regulated prospects and a standard security review workflow.
- We’ll coordinate a single thread for evidence requests to reduce cycle time.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Share the vertical Security FAQ addendum (FinServ or Healthcare).
- Offer a 30-minute structured questionnaire review call.
Guardrails
- Don’t share restricted evidence outside the approved process (NDA gates).
Pull in
- Kevin Osei, Daniel Carter (questionnaire support), Olga Petrov

3) “Can you sign a DPA? For Healthcare, can you sign a BAA?”
What to say
- We regularly work through DPAs as part of enterprise contracting. For BAA/HIPAA-related workflows, we’ll align with Legal and Security on scope, deployment mode, and required controls.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Offer to loop in Sofia Mendes (Commercial counsel) early once they confirm PHI scope + deployment preference.
Guardrails
- Don’t say “yes, we sign BAAs” as a blanket statement in an email without Legal’s involvement. Keep it as “we can review and align on requirements.”
Pull in
- Sofia Mendes, Dr. Aisha Rahman, Olga Petrov

4) “We require vendor risk artifacts: pen test summary, vuln management policy, incident response, subprocessor list.”
What to say
- We can provide vendor risk artifacts through our standard security review process and will be transparent about what we can share under NDA.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Offer a checklist-driven exchange: what they need for stage 1 vs stage 2 approval.
Guardrails
- Don’t commit to delivering any specific artifact or timeline without checking Security bandwidth/availability.
Pull in
- Marcus Lin, Olga Petrov, Kevin Osei

5) “What’s your incident notification timeline and process?”
What to say
- We have an incident response process with defined escalation and customer communications; specifics can be reviewed in security diligence and reflected in contract terms depending on tier.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Point to security review call and contractual SLA discussion.
Guardrails
- Don’t promise notification windows in writing unless they’re part of an approved template or contract language.
Pull in
- Dr. Aisha Rahman, Sofia Mendes

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PERSONA: Platform Engineering / Infrastructure

1) “We need Private in our VPC. What are the networking requirements (peering, DNS, TLS, egress)?”
What to say
- Redwood Private supports VPC-style deployment patterns with explicit network boundaries. We’ll align on connectivity (peering/private link/VPN), DNS, TLS termination, and allowlisting.
- We have a reference architecture that covers common regulated patterns including SIEM export and KMS integration points.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Share the Private/VPC reference architecture.
- Ask: cloud provider, VPC CIDRs, preferred connectivity model, outbound egress rules, certificate management process.
Guardrails
- Don’t commit to a specific connectivity method as universally supported; confirm environment constraints.
Pull in
- Simran Kaur, Colin O’Donnell, Fatima Noor

2) “How do you handle authn/authz? We need SSO, RBAC, and auditability.”
What to say
- Redwood supports enterprise auth patterns (SSO) and role-based access controls; we can map roles to least-privilege operational workflows.
- Access and admin actions can be audited.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Use approved language in the Security FAQ addendum (don’t invent RBAC scopes).
Guardrails
- Don’t claim “fine-grained RBAC for everything” unless confirmed. Say “RBAC with defined roles/scopes; we can share details.”
Pull in
- Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Markus Klein

3) “What are your SLOs? We need predictable throughput and latency.”
What to say
- Redwood is optimized for production inference economics: predictable latency/throughput via dedicated capacity, smart routing, and runtime optimizations.
- For regulated workloads, Dedicated or Private is usually the right fit to avoid noisy neighbors and to meet steady SLOs.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Ask for: model, expected TPS, context length distribution, peak concurrency, streaming needs.
- Offer a sizing workshop and POC success criteria template.
Guardrails
- Don’t promise exact latency numbers without workload details. Use ranges only if approved and tied to a scoped POC.
Pull in
- Markus Klein, Fatima Noor, Avery Johnson (AE)

4) “Operationally: who patches what? How do upgrades/rollbacks work?”
What to say
- We support controlled rollouts and version pinning to reduce risk. In Private deployments we plan upgrades with you (maintenance windows, validation, rollback plan).
Follow-ups / evidence
- Use the Private reference architecture + SE talk track. Offer a change management walkthrough.
Guardrails
- Don’t state “automatic upgrades” for Private unless the specific customer wants it and it’s supported contractually.
Pull in
- Colin O’Donnell, Simran Kaur

5) “We need logs/metrics/traces into our observability stack.”
What to say
- Redwood provides operational telemetry; in Private/VPC deployments we can route logs/metrics to customer-controlled systems depending on architecture.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Ask which stack: Datadog, Prometheus/Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Splunk.
Guardrails
- Don’t promise a specific exporter/agent if not confirmed; keep it as “supported integration patterns.”
Pull in
- Fatima Noor, Marcus Lin

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PERSONA: ML Engineering / Applied AI

1) “We care about quality regression. How do we prevent model/prompt changes from breaking things?”
What to say
- Redwood supports model versioning and rollout controls (e.g., canary, A/B) and encourages eval-driven deployments.
- We can align on a POC plan that includes your prompt sets and quality checks.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Offer to review their eval harness / golden prompts; propose a simple acceptance suite for the POC.
Guardrails
- Don’t claim fully automated eval tooling if it’s not in the product scope they’ll use; keep it to supported workflows and what SE can help set up.
Pull in
- Fatima Noor, Markus Klein

2) “Cost is unpredictable with LLMs. How do you reduce unit cost without hurting latency?”
What to say
- Redwood focuses on production economics: batching/caching strategies, routing/fallback options, and deployment choices (Dedicated/Private) to control variance.
- We’ll baseline your workload and then apply levers with measurable before/after.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Ask for: token distribution, context lengths, streaming vs non-streaming, concurrency.
- Offer a 2–3 week scoped eval with a cost/latency scorecard.
Guardrails
- Don’t promise “X% cost reduction” without benchmarking their workload.
Pull in
- SE team; for deeper runtime questions route to applied ML/engineering through Markus

3) “We need tool/function calling and structured outputs. Is that supported?”
What to say
- Redwood supports common production patterns like streaming responses and structured output workflows. We’ll confirm compatibility with your target models and payload format.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Ask which SDK and schema; offer a sample integration snippet during POC.
Guardrails
- Don’t commit to every model having identical tool-calling semantics. Confirm with the target model + version.
Pull in
- Markus Klein / Fatima Noor

4) “We need model flexibility. We might switch models quarterly.”
What to say
- Redwood is designed to make serving flexible across a changing model landscape. We can plan for model changes with pinned versions, controlled rollouts, and fallback policies.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Ask their preferred model families and constraints (license, hardware, quantization tolerance).
Guardrails
- Don’t promise a specific model onboarding timeline without checking with the model onboarding process.
Pull in
- SE + product (if model onboarding is a dependency)

5) “We need data privacy guarantees for training—do you train on our data?”
What to say
- Redwood does not use customer inputs to train customer-specific models without explicit agreement; we’ll walk through the data handling terms and the controls by deployment mode.
Follow-ups / evidence
- Provide the approved FAQ language (don’t paraphrase).
Guardrails
- Don’t introduce new contractual language; keep it to “covered by our terms / can be addressed in the DPA.”
Pull in
- Olga Petrov + Sofia Mendes if contract language is required

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Vertical-specific add-ons (use selectively)

FinServ (payments/wealth/banking) — common angles
- “We need tenant isolation and predictable performance for customer-facing workloads.” → Recommend Dedicated/Private; emphasize isolation + SLO control.
- “We have strict audit requirements and change management.” → Emphasize version pinning, controlled rollouts, auditable admin actions.
Reference
- confluence:sales-enablement/security-faq/abm-finserv-security-faq-addendum

Healthcare (provider/payer/healthtech) — common angles
- “PHI can’t leave our controlled environment.” → Recommend Private/VPC; align to minimum necessary access principles and clear data boundaries.
- “We need a path to BAA / HIPAA-aligned process.” → Route to Legal + Security; avoid blanket claims.
Reference
- confluence:sales-enablement/security-faq/abm-healthcare-security-faq-addendum

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Email/snippet-ready short answers (copy/paste)

A) Data retention (safe default)
“Happy to walk through our data handling by deployment mode and your preferred logging configuration. For regulated workloads we can align retention to operational needs and support exporting audit logs into customer-controlled systems. We’ll share questionnaire-ready details in a security review.”

B) Private/VPC default
“For sensitive data and stricter residency/audit requirements, we typically recommend Redwood Private in your VPC so you control network boundaries while keeping a consistent inference API and operations model.”

C) KMS/HSM default
“We can align to customer key management requirements in Private/VPC contexts. Let’s confirm your KMS/HSM policy (provider, rotation, separation-of-duties) and map it to our reference architecture.”
